title: Thune Forces Government Funding Showdown, Threatens to Hold Budget Resolution
excerpt: Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he will put a stopgap spending bill on the Senate floor before the August recess and hold up the House's budget resolution until government funding is resolved.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Senate will vote on a continuing resolution before the August 6 recess.
  • Thune threatens to hold House's $95 billion budget resolution until funding is resolved.
  • House narrowly advanced a funding package with a 214-211 vote.
  • Congress faces pressure to avoid shutdowns ahead of November midterms.
  • Democrats oppose the continuing resolution over funding flexibility concerns.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune announced the Senate will vote on a continuing resolution before the August recess begins on August 6.
  • Thune threatened to use reconciliation to fund the government if necessary and will hold the House's $95 billion budget resolution until funding is settled.
  • The House cleared a key procedural vote 214-211 on Tuesday, advancing a stopgap bill to keep agencies funded through December 4, along with the NDAA and a budget resolution.
  • Congress has endured two record-breaking shutdowns since the start of Trump's second term, and Republicans are eager to avoid another ahead of November's midterms.
https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2079578263760916732

Thune Draws a Line on Government Funding

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) escalated a high-stakes funding standoff on Tuesday, declaring that the Senate will vote on a continuing resolution before lawmakers leave for their August break and threatening to hold up the House's budget resolution until government funding is resolved.

According to Politico reporter Laura Weiss, Thune also raised the prospect of using reconciliation — a powerful legislative tool that bypasses the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold — to fund the government if necessary. The threat to hold the House's $95 billion budget resolution, which would unlock spending on defense, farm aid, and the SAVE America Act, gives Thune substantial leverage over Speaker Mike Johnson.

"We've got to figure out how to get 50 votes for it. That will be easier said than done."

— Sen. John Thune, Senate Majority Leader

House Clears Narrow Procedural Vote

> **"Republicans are acutely aware another lapse could devastate their midterm prospects.

"It takes away the leverage point for midterms to shut down the government."**

Thune's announcement came as House Republicans narrowly cleared a procedural hurdle on Tuesday, voting 214-211 to advance a package that includes the National Defense Authorization Act, the continuing resolution, a stock trading ban, and the budget resolution.

The razor-thin margin underscored the fragility of Speaker Johnson's 218-212 majority. The vote only succeeded after last-minute lobbying on the House floor, where Johnson and Majority Whip Tom Emmer huddled with holdout conservatives including Reps. Lauren Boebert (R-CO), Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL), and Tim Burchett (R-TN). Democrats are expected to unanimously oppose the package.

The continuing resolution would fund the government through December 4 — safely past the November midterm elections. Current funding expires on September 30.

A Shutdown-Scarred Congress

The urgency is shaped by brutal recent history. Congress has endured two record-breaking shutdowns since the start of Trump's second term: a 43-day full shutdown ending last November and a 76-day partial shutdown ending in April. Republicans are acutely aware another lapse could devastate their midterm prospects.

"It takes away the leverage point for midterms to shut down the government. Shutting down the government is not what the people want."

— Rep. Rich McCormick (R-GA)

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole (R-OK) echoed the urgency: "We have to move. We want to make sure we don't shut down the government. The right thing to do is to get a CR in place and continue to negotiate."

House-Senate Tensions and Democratic Opposition

Thune's maneuvering also reflects a widening rift between House and Senate Republican leadership. Last week, when Johnson suggested both chambers would pass a third reconciliation package before the recess, Thune publicly rebuffed the idea, telling reporters it was "news to me." The Senate's deliberations have been further complicated by the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), who chaired the Budget Committee.

Democrats, meanwhile, have signaled they will oppose the CR over language they say gives Customs and Border Protection unauthorized flexibility to transfer funds. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (D-CA) cited "drafting errors" that allow CBP to "move money around," violating a previous bipartisan agreement.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

For the growing number of Indian Americans in the federal workforce — across agencies from NASA to the State Department — another shutdown carries real financial consequences. The two recent shutdowns left hundreds of thousands of employees furloughed or working without guaranteed pay, disrupting visa processing at U.S. consulates and research grants at federal laboratories.

What's Next

The House is expected to vote on the CR Tuesday night, followed by the budget resolution Wednesday, before departing Thursday. The Senate, which breaks August 6, will then take up the stopgap bill. If the process stalls, Thune's threat to use reconciliation as a funding backstop could reshape the legislative landscape heading into the midterms.
